page.title: Help
page.subtitle: Everything you need to use Nebulis, from first install to everyday use.

whatIsNebulis.title: What is Nebulis
whatIsNebulis.lead: Your astrophotography library and session planner, running on your own machine.
whatIsNebulis.p1: Connect a smart telescope and Nebulis pulls in every session automatically, building one library sorted by object and by night, with full capture history, FITS metadata, and your own notes attached. Check the Forecast before you head out for a single sky score built from cloud cover, seeing, and moon phase, then use the Planner to turn your object list into a real schedule for the hours you have.
whatIsNebulis.p2: It doesn't edit, stack, or control your telescope. Those jobs already have tools built for them. Nebulis is what happens after: everything your gear captured, finally organized into something you can actually use.
whatIsNebulis.runsLocally: Runs entirely on your own computer. Every image stays on hardware you own, for as long as you want it.

quickAnswers.title: Quick answers
quickAnswers.subtitle: The things most people want to know first.

sendImages.q: Does Nebulis send my images anywhere?
sendImages.a: No. Nebulis runs on your own machine and your images stay there. Nothing leaves your network unless you choose to share it.

whichTelescopes.a: ZWO SeeStar S30, S30 Pro, S50, and S50 Pro, the ZWO ASIAIR, and DWARFLAB Dwarf 3, Dwarf II, and Dwarf Mini. There is also a generic option for any SMB share that follows the same folder layout, such as a NAS or another camera.

firstSteps.q: I just installed it. What do I do first?
firstSteps.a: Create your account, add a telescope under Settings → Telescopes, set your location under Settings → Sky, then run an import. That is the whole setup.

newImages.q: How do new images get into my library?
newImages.a: Sync from the telescope icon in the top bar, or turn on auto-import in Settings → Telescopes. You can also import files you already have from a folder.

viewOnPhone.q: Can I view my library on a phone or TV?
viewOnPhone.a: Yes. Nebulis has iOS, Apple TV, and Android apps that connect to your server over the same network. Pair them under Settings → Account → Devices.

objectFilters.q: What does each object filter include?
objectFilters.a: Filters group objects by their catalog type, matching the type text itself. Those type names come from the catalog and stay in English whatever language you use, so the words that matter are "galaxy", "nebula" and "cluster". Any type containing "galaxy" lands in the galaxy filter: spiral, barred, irregular, lenticular and starburst galaxies, plus galaxy groups, pairs and triplets. "nebula" covers emission, reflection, dark and planetary nebulae, and supernova remnants count as nebulae too. "cluster" covers open and globular clusters. An object can appear under more than one filter: a planetary nebula is both a nebula and a planetary nebula, a supernova remnant is both a nebula and a supernova remnant, and Cluster + Nebula is both a cluster and a nebula. Where a count has to choose one family, Cluster + Nebula counts as a nebula, because the nebulosity is what it is imaged for. The Library adds finer filters on top: solar system objects, comets, stars, planetary nebulae, supernova remnants, and Unknown, which holds objects whose type could not be resolved.

locationSharing.q: Does Nebulis send my location anywhere?
locationSharing.a: Only to fetch conditions for your sky. Your observing site's coordinates go to Open-Meteo and 7Timer for the forecast, and to DarkSkySites for your light pollution class. Those are the coordinates of the site you set up in Settings, not your device's location, and nothing else about you is included. Every service Nebulis uses is listed under Settings, Data Sources.

gettingStarted.title: Getting started
gettingStarted.lead: You are already signed in, so start with the telescope. Then set where you observe and pull your first night.
gettingStarted.step1Body: Open Settings → Telescopes → Add smart telescope. Pick your model and enter the address. The share name and other defaults fill in on their own.
gettingStarted.step1AltA: Settings → Telescopes, with the Add smart telescope button at the bottom of the list
gettingStarted.step1AltB: The Add Smart Telescope dialog, with telescope type, display name, badge color, and connection fields
gettingStarted.step2Body: Settings → Sky → your observing site. Latitude, longitude, and timezone are required for the Planner and Forecast to do anything useful.
gettingStarted.step2Alt: Settings → Sky, showing an observing site with its name, coordinates, and minimum altitude
gettingStarted.step3Body: Open the telescope icon in the top bar and choose Sync. The first run copies everything, so it is the slowest one. Later runs only move new files.
gettingStarted.step3Alt: The telescope pill in the top bar, open to show each telescope with a Sync button and a Sync all option

tour.title: A tour of the app
tour.lead: Learn what each page does and how to use it.
tour.body: Select a page from the menu on the left to learn what it does, why you'd use it, and how to get the most out of it.

tourLibrary.title: Library
tourLibrary.lead: Your home base. Every object you have imaged shows as a card with its best photo.
tourLibrary.step1Body: Type a catalog ID like M51, a common name like Whirlpool, or a constellation. Tap the filter icon to show only the object types you care about: galaxies, nebulae, clusters, whatever you want to focus on.
tourLibrary.step1Alt: The Library page with the Customize filters menu open, listing object type groups as checkboxes
tourLibrary.step2Body: Tap any card to see every session you've imaged it in. You get the date, telescope, number of sub-frames, file size, and a timeline of your progress. Mark it as a favorite by starring it. Your best captures show at the top when you filter for Favorites.
tourLibrary.step2Alt: The Library page showing object cards with thumbnails, object names, and session information
tourLibrary.step3Body: Open an object, tap Notes, and log your personal rating, seeing quality, Bortle class, location, equipment used, and any thoughts about the session. These notes attach to that session permanently so you can reference them anytime.
tourLibrary.step3Alt: The Session Notes dialog filled in with a personal rating, seeing rating, Bortle class, location, equipment, and notes
tourLibrary.step4Body: On an object's page, use the action bar to Download all frames as a ZIP, Combine subs to stack your raw frames into one image, or Upload your finished processed image to use as the thumbnail. Once you have a final stack, delete the raw sub-frames to free up disk space while keeping the stacked result and all metadata.
tourLibrary.step4Alt: An object page's action bar, with Add observation, Plan a night, Compare, Combine subs, and Download buttons
tourLibrary.step5Body: Go to Settings → Storage to see a full breakdown of which objects are using the most disk space, sorted largest first. This makes it easy to find and manage the heavy ones when you need to free up room.
tourLibrary.step5Alt: The Storage page, showing overall disk usage and a per-object breakdown table sorted by total size

tourObjects.title: Object Details
tourObjects.lead: View all your imaging history for a specific object. Track sessions, metadata, processed images, and visibility forecasts in one place.
tourObjects.step1Title: View your best capture and object info
tourObjects.step1Body: Click any object in your Library to open its detail page. At the top, you see your best captured image displayed prominently, along with all the object's catalog information: its type (galaxy, nebula, cluster, etc.), constellation, coordinates (RA/Dec), visual magnitude, distance in light-years, and angular size. A star icon lets you quickly add the object to your favorites for easy access.
tourObjects.step1Alt: Object detail page showing the best captured image, object name, and catalog metadata
tourObjects.step2Title: Check tonight's visibility and weather forecasts
tourObjects.step2Body: Just below the image, you'll see a "Tonight" panel showing whether this object is visible from your observing location and when it's best to image. It displays the current altitude, the peak altitude and when it happens, an altitude curve for the night, and the best months of the year to shoot it. This helps you plan your observing session in advance.
tourObjects.step2Alt: Tonight visibility panel showing an altitude curve, current altitude, and best months to image
tourObjects.step3Title: Browse the finished images from any session
tourObjects.step3Body: Click into a session to see its Images tab: the finished stack and its FITS master side by side, with All / Image / Fits filters to switch between them. A Processed tab next to it holds any JPG, PNG, or TIFF finals you have uploaded for that night, separate from the raw stack.
tourObjects.step3Alt: A session's Images tab showing the JPG stack and FITS master with All, Image, and Fits filter buttons
tourObjects.step4Body: Further down is a complete history of every session you've imaged this object in, grouped by year and sorted newest first. Each card shows the date captured, telescope used, how many sub-frames were stacked, cloud cover, and temperature that night. Click any card to open the full session, its raw sub-frames, and its FITS metadata.
tourObjects.step4Alt: Observations section showing session cards grouped by year with date, telescope, and weather
tourObjects.step5Body: For each session, you can tap the Notes icon to record your personal experience from that night. Log your seeing rating (1-5 stars), sky darkness (Bortle scale), observing location, equipment used, weather conditions, and any thoughts about the imaging run. These notes stay permanently attached to that session so you can remember what worked well and what to try differently next time.
tourObjects.step5Alt: Session notes form showing star rating, seeing, Bortle, location, and equipment fields
tourObjects.note: All session notes, metadata, and observations stay permanently attached to their object. Revisit any object years later and you'll still have exactly what you captured, what equipment you used, and your thoughts from that observing session.

tourGallery.title: Gallery
tourGallery.lead: Every frame from your library in one grid, with a filter to narrow it down to just your finished results.
tourGallery.step1Title: Browse every frame, or just the processed ones
tourGallery.step1Body: The header shows totals for images, objects, processed finals, and favorites. By default the grid includes every frame in your library; turn on Processed only to see just the JPG, PNG, and TIFF finals you've uploaded. Search by object name, filter by object type, or sort the grid to find what you're after.
tourGallery.step1Alt: Image Gallery page showing header stats and a grid of thumbnails, with Favorites, Processed only, and object-type filters
tourGallery.step2Body: Click any thumbnail to open it in a full-screen viewer. Toggle between Fit and 1:1 to zoom in on detail, favorite or share the image, and download it. A filmstrip along the bottom lets you jump between every image for that object without closing the viewer.
tourGallery.step2Alt: Full-size image viewer for the Eagle Nebula with Fit, 1:1, favorite, share, and download controls, and a filmstrip of other images below
tourGallery.step3Body: Search narrows the grid to one object's frames across every session. Hover a thumbnail to favorite it right from the grid, or click through to see which object and session produced it. Favorites and Processed only combine with search, so you can find a specific final fast even in a large library.
tourGallery.step3Alt: Gallery filtered by search to Eagle Nebula, with a favorite heart icon showing on hover over the first thumbnail
tourGallery.note: Your Gallery automatically updates as you import new frames or upload processed images from any object or session. It's a living collection of your astrophotography achievements.

tourObservations.title: Observations
tourObservations.lead: Every imaging session you've ever logged, browsable by calendar, list, or map.
tourObservations.step1Title: See your imaging activity at a glance
tourObservations.step1Body: The header totals nights out, distinct objects, sessions, and files across your whole history, and a bar chart breaks sessions down by month for the selected year. Below it, the Calendar view lays out every session on the day it happened, with a thumbnail and time for each object.
tourObservations.step1Alt: Observations page showing lifetime totals, a monthly bar chart, and a calendar grid with session thumbnails on each day
tourObservations.step2Title: Switch to a list, or a map of where you've observed
tourObservations.step2Body: The List view is a sortable table of every session by object, catalog id, and date, good for scanning a long history fast. Filter either view down to one telescope with the scope dropdown, and use Share to hand someone a read-only link.
tourObservations.step2Alt: Observations List view showing a sortable table of sessions with Object, Catalog, and Date columns
tourObservations.step3Body: Click any session to open its full detail page: the stacked image, integration time, frames stacked, exposure and filter used, plus panels for the object itself, sky conditions that night, and where you observed from. Add notes, combine subs, or delete the session from here.
tourObservations.step3Alt: M45 Pleiades observation detail page showing the stacked image, integration stats, and About, Conditions, and Observed from panels
tourObservations.step4Body: The Map view plots every session by location, clustered by how many you logged nearby. If you observe from more than one site, home, a dark-sky trip, a friend's backyard, this is the fastest way to see your history spread across them.
tourObservations.step4Alt: Observations Map view showing session location clusters across the southeastern United States
tourObservations.note: Every observation is permanently linked to its object. Even years later, you'll be able to see exactly what you captured, when, with which equipment, and under what conditions.

tourForecast.title: Forecast
tourForecast.lead: A single 0–100 score for tonight, plus the astronomical facts and weather behind it.
tourForecast.step1Title: Read tonight's score at a glance
tourForecast.step1Body: The ring on the left boils cloud cover, seeing and jet stream, and moon interference down to one 0–100 rating with a plain-language verdict underneath. Dark hours, sunset, sunrise, and the best imaging window sit alongside it, and the ribbon below traces sky quality through the night, worst to best, so you can see exactly when it gets good.
tourForecast.step1Alt: Sky Forecast page showing a 55/100 Good rating, moon phase, dark hours, sunset and sunrise times, best window, and a colored night-quality ribbon
tourForecast.step2Body: Below the ribbon, "The nights ahead" cards give each upcoming night its own score and a cloud-cover trend line, so you can tell at a glance whether tomorrow is worth staying up for or better spent processing what you already have.
tourForecast.step2Alt: Two upcoming-night cards showing a 64 Good score for Thursday and a 94 Excellent score for Friday, each with a cloud cover trend line
tourForecast.step3Body: If you've set up more than one site under Settings → Sky, the location picker in the top right switches the whole forecast between them instantly. Handy for comparing home against a dark-sky spot before deciding where to drive.
tourForecast.step3Alt: Location picker open showing Franklin Tennessee, Nashville - West, and Russia as selectable observing sites
tourForecast.note: Forecast data comes from open-meteo and 7Timer, combined into one score tuned for imaging rather than general weather.

tourPlanner.title: Planner
tourPlanner.lead: Build tonight's schedule target by target, and watch conflicts and free time update as you go.
tourPlanner.step1Title: Add targets to build your schedule
tourPlanner.step1Body: Search or browse the Targets list on the left, each one shows its magnitude, constellation, and when it peaks tonight, and tap + to drop it onto the Night schedule on the right. Nebulis picks a sensible time window automatically; drag a block's handle to nudge it, or use the day picker up top to plan any of the next two weeks.
tourPlanner.step1Alt: Planner page with three targets added to the night schedule, showing scheduled time blocks and remaining free time
tourPlanner.step2Title: See exactly when each target is well placed
tourPlanner.step2Body: Scroll down and the altitude chart plots a curve for every scheduled target across the night, shaded over the span it's actually booked for. It's the fastest way to check a target isn't scheduled while it's still low on the horizon.
tourPlanner.step2Alt: Altitude curve chart showing three scheduled targets with their curves shaded over their booked time windows
tourPlanner.step3Body: If two targets land in the same window, their blocks sit side by side in the schedule instead of stacking, an unmistakable sign you've overcommitted the night. Drag one to a free slot, or remove it with the × on the card.
tourPlanner.step3Alt: Night schedule showing two targets both booked for 22:20 to 23:50, their blocks placed side by side to flag the overlap
tourPlanner.step4Title: Check the moon and darkness for the night
tourPlanner.step4Body: The header sums up the night before you add anything: a Fair/Good/Excellent score, moon phase and illumination with its set time, and how many objects out of your whole catalog are visible tonight. Plan my night can fill the schedule for you from there.
tourPlanner.step4Alt: Planner header showing a Fair score, Waxing Gibbous moon at 61% illuminated, and a Plan my night button
tourPlanner.note: A well-organized plan means you'll spend less time searching for targets and more time imaging. Use the planner to maximize your productive observing hours.

tourCatalogs.title: Catalogs
tourCatalogs.lead: Track your progress through classic observing programs, and research your next target.
tourCatalogs.step1Title: Pick a catalog to work through
tourCatalogs.step1Body: Catalogs opens on a scoreboard: how many unique objects you've imaged across every catalog combined, then a card for each one, Messier, Caldwell, Herschel 400, Sharpless, with its imaged percentage and a breakdown by galaxies, nebulae, clusters, and other. Open a board to start working through it.
tourCatalogs.step1Alt: Catalogs landing page showing overall progress and catalog cards for Messier, Caldwell, Herschel 400, and Sharpless with imaged percentages
tourCatalogs.step2Title: Browse a catalog and see what you still need
tourCatalogs.step2Body: Inside a board, filter to All, Imaged, or Remaining, search by name or constellation, and the grid marks every object you've already captured with a checkmark and session count. It's the fastest way to see what's left on a list like Messier or Caldwell.
tourCatalogs.step2Alt: Messier catalog board showing progress bars by object type and a grid of objects with checkmarks and session counts on imaged ones
tourCatalogs.step3Title: Look up an object before you shoot it
tourCatalogs.step3Body: Click any entry to open a quick-reference card: type, constellation, magnitude, coordinates, a description with a Wikipedia link, and a bar chart of its maximum altitude for each of the next 12 months so you know which season suits it best.
tourCatalogs.step3Alt: M16 Eagle Nebula quick reference card showing a description, Wikipedia link, and a monthly max-altitude bar chart with Feb through Oct highlighted as the best window
tourCatalogs.step4Title: Jump straight to observing or planning it
tourCatalogs.step4Body: From that same card, View observations takes you to everything you've already captured of it, and Open in Planner drops it onto tonight's schedule. Objects you've already imaged carry their session count right in the grid, so you always know where you stand before you commit a night to it.
tourCatalogs.step4Alt: Catalog grid showing checkmark badges and session counts on imaged objects like Pleiades (17 sessions) and Orion Nebula (13 sessions)
tourCatalogs.note: Catalog entries carry distance and angular size where known, so you can also just browse for objects that happen to be nearby or a good match for your telescope's field of view.

tourSettings.title: Settings
tourSettings.lead: Configure your app, manage storage, connect devices, and control your Nebulis experience.
tourSettings.step1Title: Set your theme, units, and navigation
tourSettings.step1Body: Settings → General covers the look and feel of the app: Light, Dark, Space, or Night theme, which menu items show in the top bar, measurement units, and other library defaults.
tourSettings.step1Alt: Settings → General, showing theme options (Light, Dark, Space, Night) and navigation bar toggles
tourSettings.step2Title: Manage your account and connected devices
tourSettings.step2Body: In Settings → Account, manage users (admin or viewer) and see every phone, tablet, or TV paired to your library. Connect a device to generate a QR code for quick pairing, and revoke access for any device you no longer use.
tourSettings.step2Alt: Settings → Account → Devices, with a Connect a device button and an empty device list
tourSettings.step3Body: Add your smart telescopes, cameras, or network sources. Support includes ZWO SeeStar, ZWO ASIAIR, DWARFLAB Dwarf series, and standard SMB network shares. For each telescope, configure the connection type (Wi-Fi or USB), network settings, and enable/disable to control syncing. Automatically discover nearby devices or manually enter connection details.
tourSettings.step3Alt: Telescopes settings showing list of connected devices with connection status
tourSettings.step4Body: Settings → Sky is where the Planner and Forecast get their facts: your observing site's coordinates and timezone, minimum altitude, catalog source, and data sources such as satellite trail tracking.
tourSettings.step4Alt: Settings → Sky, showing an observing site with its name, coordinates, and minimum altitude
tourSettings.step5Body: Check your total library storage usage and see a breakdown by object. Find which objects are using the most disk space. Move your library to a different drive or network location if needed. Manage your backups and set automated backup schedules to protect your imaging data.
tourSettings.step5Alt: Storage settings showing total usage, per-object breakdown, and library location controls
tourSettings.step6Title: Connect other devices and manage pairing
tourSettings.step6Body: Pair your iPad, iPhone, Apple TV, or web browsers to access your library remotely. Generate QR codes for quick pairing, view all connected devices, and revoke access from devices you no longer use. Each device gets its own authentication token for secure access.
tourSettings.step6Alt: Devices settings showing list of paired devices with revoke buttons
tourSettings.step7Body: Access advanced settings like enabling night mode (red-tinted interface for dark adaptation), adjusting satellite trail detection sensitivity, clearing cached data, resetting the app, and viewing logs. Export your data or import previously backed up libraries.
tourSettings.step7Alt: Advanced settings showing theme options, data management, and expert controls
tourSettings.note: Settings is where you can fine-tune Nebulis to match your exact workflow. Most settings take effect immediately, though some (like telescope connections) may require a resync.

telescopes.title: Adding a telescope or source
telescopes.lead: Nebulis reads files over Wi-Fi or USB, and it can also read a plain folder shared on your network.
telescopes.seestarTerm: ZWO SeeStar S30, S30 Pro, S50, and S50 Pro
telescopes.seestarDef: Wi-Fi over SMB, or USB when the storage is plugged in directly.
telescopes.smbDef: A NAS, PC, or another camera that follows the <1>custom SMB folder layout</1>.
telescopes.step1Title: Go to Settings → Telescopes → Add smart telescope.
telescopes.step2Body: The share name, username, and defaults fill in automatically.
telescopes.step3Title: Choose how to connect, then Test Connection.
telescopes.note: You can add more than one telescope. Each imports on its own, and the icon in the top bar shows how many are online.
telescopes.altAddSmartTelescope: The Add Smart Telescope dialog with the Telescope Type dropdown set to ZWO SeeStar S50

customSmb.title: Custom SMB sources
customSmb.lead: A NAS, a PC share, or any camera works as a source as long as its files are organized the way Nebulis expects.
customSmb.introBefore: Add it under Settings → Telescopes → Add smart telescope, with the telescope type set to
customSmb.introAfter: Then lay out the share root like this:
customSmb.folderTree:
<share root>/
└── M31/                       one folder per object: a catalog id (M31, NGC1788) or a common name
    ├── 2026-04-26_2030/       session folder, local time: <YYYY-MM-DD>_<HHMM>
    │   ├── lights/            required: at least one stacked or single-shot final
    │   │   ├── M31_stacked.fit
    │   │   └── M31_stacked.jpg
    │   ├── subframes/         optional: individual sub-frames
    │   │   ├── M31_001.fit
    │   │   └── M31_002.fit
    │   └── meta.json          optional: exposureSec, gain, filter, frameCount, integrationSec
    └── 2026-05-03_2115/
        └── lights/...
customSmb.objectFolderDef: Its name is the catalog id or common name Nebulis will file everything under. A recognized catalog id resolves to better metadata than a plain common name.
customSmb.sessionFolderDef: Must match YYYY-MM-DD_HHMM exactly, in local time. The date drives the calendar view; the time keeps two sessions on the same night apart.
customSmb.lightsDef: Required. At least one finished image, FITS master, or single-shot capture. A session folder with no files here is skipped entirely, so a half-finished copy never creates an empty object.
customSmb.subframesDef: Optional. Individual sub-frames for quality scoring and per-frame review. Only pulled in when "Include subframes" is turned on for this source, same as any other telescope.
customSmb.metaJsonDef: Optional. A small JSON file with whatever you know: exposureSec, gain, filter, frameCount, integrationSec. Leave out anything you don't have.
customSmb.filenamesDef: Not parsed at all. Nebulis decides what a file is by which folder it sits in, not by what it's called, so anything with a supported extension in lights/ or subframes/ is picked up.
customSmb.note: Already have files sitting directly inside the object folder with no session subfolders? That still works exactly as before, everything lands in one flat folder for that object. The session-folder layout above is only needed when you want each night kept separate, with sub-frames and metadata alongside it.

importing.title: Importing and syncing images
importing.lead: Importing copies new files from your telescope into the library. Files you have already imported are skipped, so re-running is safe.
importing.bullet1: Sync now: click the telescope icon in the top bar and pick Sync, or use the refresh button on a telescope in Settings. The icon also shows how many telescopes are currently online.
importing.bullet2: Auto-import: turn it on for a telescope in Settings → Telescopes, and Nebulis pulls new captures on a schedule with no clicking needed.
importing.bullet3: First import: the first run copies everything, so give it a few minutes. Later runs only move new files.
importing.altSyncDropdown: The telescope pill in the top bar, open to show each telescope with a Sync button and a Sync all option
importing.altBackupStatus: The Backup Status page, showing per-telescope sync state and a history of past syncs
importing.note: Watch progress on the Backup page. It keeps a row for every import with how many files moved, how long it took, and any errors.

uploading.title: Uploading images
uploading.lead: Not everything has to come straight from a telescope. You can bring in files you already have, or log a session by hand.
uploading.bullet1: Upload files: Library → Upload Files. Drag in a folder from your computer, or pick a folder already on the server. You review each object before anything is committed.
uploading.bullet2: Add a processed image: open a session and upload your finished JPG, PNG, or TIFF. It becomes the card thumbnail and shows in the slideshow.
uploading.bullet3: Log an observation: Library → New Observation. Record a session manually with an optional image and notes.
uploading.altUploadFiles: The Import to Library dialog, with a drop zone for a folder and options for subframes and archiving everything
uploading.altNewObservation: The Log Observation dialog, with fields for object, date, image, telescope, and notes

manualImport.title: Manual imports from a folder
manualImport.lead: Point Nebulis at a folder that's already sitting somewhere, either on the computer running Nebulis or on a network share, instead of dragging files through the browser.
manualImport.step1Body: The same dialog used for a browser upload has a second path down at the bottom for files that are already somewhere Nebulis can reach.
manualImport.step1Alt: The Import to Library dialog's drop zone, with a link below it reading 'Files already on the computer running Nebulis? Import in place, no upload.'
manualImport.step2Title: Click "Files already on the computer running Nebulis?"
manualImport.step2Body: This switches to a server-side folder browser: pick a drive Nebulis can see, or type a path directly. Nothing uploads. The server reads the folder where it already sits, so even a huge backup imports in seconds instead of streaming through your browser.
manualImport.step2Alt: The server-side folder picker, listing detected drives and an 'Or enter a path' field with a placeholder showing a UNC path and a drive letter path
manualImport.step3Title: For a NAS or network folder, type its UNC path.
manualImport.step3Body: A network share never shows up in the drive list above, and a mapped drive letter (like <1>Z:</1>) won't work either. Both only exist inside your own sign-in session, and Nebulis runs as a background service that doesn't share it. Type or paste the share's full UNC path instead, for example <3>\\NAS-OBSERVATORY\Astrophotography</3>, and Nebulis browses it the same way as a local drive.
manualImport.step3Alt: The folder picker with a UNC path opened, showing its subfolders SeeStar S50, Dwarf 3, and _archive
manualImport.step3Caption: Upload Files → Import in place → UNC path
manualImport.step4Body: Same review step as any other import: Nebulis shows every object, session, and file it found before anything is committed, so nothing lands in the library unreviewed.
manualImport.note: If typing the UNC path fails with a permission or "cannot read that folder" error, the share itself is reachable but Nebulis isn't allowed onto it yet. See below.

giveAccess.title: Give Nebulis access to that network share
giveAccess.lead: A UNC path only resolves if whatever is running Nebulis is already allowed onto the share, the same way a person would need to be. Nebulis itself has no login prompt for this: it inherits access from the account its background process runs as, so that account is what needs to be squared away with the NAS or PC sharing the folder.
giveAccess.note: A share configured for guest or anonymous access needs none of this: it already works no matter which account Nebulis runs as. This is only for a share that asks for a username and password.

serviceAccountTabs.winIntro: Nebulis installs as a Windows service, which by default runs as <1>Local System</1>, a machine identity with no credentials on your NAS or PC. Give the service an account the share already trusts:
serviceAccountTabs.winStep1Body: Press <1>Win + R</1>, type <3>services.msc</3>, and press Enter.
serviceAccountTabs.winStep2Title: Find Nebulis, then open its Log On tab.
serviceAccountTabs.winStep2Body: Right-click <1>Nebulis</1> in the list → Properties → the <3>Log On</3> tab.
serviceAccountTabs.winStep3Title: Switch to "This account" and enter its credentials.
serviceAccountTabs.winStep3Body: Use an account the share already grants access to: a local account as <1>.\username</1>, or a domain account as <3>DOMAIN\username</3>. Enter its password, click OK, and Windows grants that account the "Log on as a service" right automatically.
serviceAccountTabs.winStep4Body: Right-click Nebulis → Restart, or from an elevated prompt: <1>net stop Nebulis && net start Nebulis</1>.
serviceAccountTabs.winFooter: Re-registered the service by hand with <1>install-service.bat</1> instead of the installer? Set the account from the command line first: <3>nssm.exe set Nebulis ObjectName ".\username" "password"</3>, then restart it the same way.
serviceAccountTabs.macIntro: The Mac build has no separate service account: Nebulis runs as a LaunchAgent inside whichever macOS user is currently logged in, so it already has that user's access. The fix here is making sure that account can reach the share, not swapping the account Nebulis uses.
serviceAccountTabs.macStep1Title: Connect to the share once from Finder.
serviceAccountTabs.macStep1Body: Press <1>Cmd + K</1> (Finder → Go → Connect to Server), enter <3>smb://host/share</3>, and sign in with the credentials the folder needs. Turn on <5>Remember this password in my keychain</5> so it reconnects on its own later.
serviceAccountTabs.macStep2Title: Use the /Volumes path, not the smb:// address.
serviceAccountTabs.macStep2Body: Once mounted it appears under <1>/Volumes/</1>, e.g. <3>/Volumes/Astrophotography</3>. That's the path to type into Nebulis's folder picker.
serviceAccountTabs.macStep3Title: Logged in as a different user than the share credentials belong to?
serviceAccountTabs.macStep3Body: Log in as (or fast-user-switch to) the macOS account that owns those credentials before opening Nebulis, since the LaunchAgent runs inside whichever account is signed in at the time.

mobileDevices.title: Mobile devices
mobileDevices.lead: iPhone, iPad, Apple TV, and Android apps that read the same library over your local network. No cloud, no subscription, no separate account to manage.
mobileDevices.step1Title: Download the app for your device
mobileDevices.step1Body: iPhone, iPad, and Apple TV share one app on the App Store; Android has its own on Google Play. Both are free and connect to this same server, so anything you capture, star, or process on the web shows up there too.
mobileDevices.step1Alt: The Mobile menu open in the top bar, showing Scan QR code, Enter code, and download links for iPhone/iPad/Apple TV and Android
mobileDevices.step2Title: Connect a phone or tablet with a QR code
mobileDevices.step2Body: Click the <1>Mobile</1> button in the top bar and choose <3>Scan QR code</3>. Open Nebulis on your phone, tap Scan QR, and point it at the code on screen. It connects and signs you in together, no typing an IP address. The code refreshes itself and expires after ten minutes if it isn't used.
mobileDevices.step2Alt: The Connect a device dialog with a QR code to scan from the Nebulis phone app, plus a manual address fallback
mobileDevices.step3Title: Link an Apple TV with a short code
mobileDevices.step3Body: A TV has no camera, so pairing works the other way around: open Nebulis on the Apple TV and it displays a four-character code. Back on the web, click <1>Mobile</1> → <3>Enter code</3>, type what's on screen, and confirm the TV name that comes up.
mobileDevices.step3Alt: The Link an Apple TV dialog with a four-character code input field
mobileDevices.step4Body: Every phone, tablet, and TV you've linked shows up under Settings → Account → Devices. Each one carries its own sign-in token, so revoking a device here cuts its access immediately without touching anyone else's.
mobileDevices.step4Alt: Settings → Account → Devices, with a Connect a device button and an empty device list

troubleshooting.title: Troubleshooting
troubleshooting.lead: The problems people actually run into.
troubleshooting.bullet1: The telescope will not connect: check both are on the same Wi-Fi, try the IP instead of the hostname, and check the share name. Use Test connection in the telescope editor to see the exact error.
troubleshooting.bullet2: An import is stuck or slow: weak Wi-Fi and large FITS files are the usual causes. Cancel and retry; it resumes where it stopped.
troubleshooting.bullet3: A new session is not showing up: clear filters in the Library, check the import log on the Backup page, then re-run the import.
troubleshooting.bullet4: The Planner is empty: almost always the location is unset or the minimum altitude is too high. Check Settings → Sky and lower it.
troubleshooting.bullet5: The library says it is unavailable: check the drive it is stored on is connected, or that the network share is reachable.

mobileAppsPromo.title: Nebulis Mobile Apps
mobileAppsPromo.heading: Nebulis on Mobile
mobileAppsPromo.subtitle: Take your library anywhere
mobileAppsPromo.body1: Thank you for using Nebulis. I believe your images and data belong to you, which is why I built this as a free, secure, self-hosted solution. Your library stays on your hardware, no accounts, no subscriptions, and no data leaving your network.
mobileAppsPromo.body2: The mobile apps let you browse your library on the go, or pull it up on your TV (Apple TV). I charge a small one-time fee ($4.99) to help cover ongoing development costs on those platforms.

whatsNewV20.title: What's new in Nebulis 2.0
whatsNewV20.subtitle: A full UI redesign, a night-first Planner and Sky Forecast, and a guided tour to get new users started.

planner.title: Planner, redesigned around picking a night
planner.lead: See two weeks at a glance.
planner.description: A two-week strip shows each night's forecast rating, Moon phase, and whether you already have a plan. The schedule reads the weather forecast hour by hour, with a twilight gradient and a line marking the current time.

forecast.title: Sky Forecast, redesigned around tonight
forecast.description: A single rating, the Moon at its real phase, and a night ribbon covering twilight, clouds, Moon-up hours, and visibility on one timeline, plus a best-window readout for the nights ahead.

catalogs.title: Sharpless joins the catalogs
catalogs.lead: A new catalog to work through.
catalogs.description: The Sharpless catalog of emission nebulae is now part of the set, alongside Messier, Caldwell, and Herschel 400. Each has a progress board showing what you've captured and what's still up, and search matches any of an object's catalog names.

observations.title: Observations, redesigned
observations.description: See your observations as a month-by-month chart, on a map, or as a list. The page opens on your nights out and your objects, and the calendar lands on your most recent night with each day showing its photo.

guidedTour.title: Guided Tour
guidedTour.description: A guided tour launches automatically on a new install and walks you through the app. Restart it anytime from Help -> Start the Guided Tour.

helpPage.title: New Help page
helpPage.description: Screenshots and walkthroughs for importing, syncing, planning, and more, all in one place.

systemLog.title: System Log for admins
systemLog.description: A searchable history of sign-ins, user changes, telescope and device changes, syncs, and settings changes. Settings -> System Log.

backupStatus.title: Backup Status, redesigned
backupStatus.description: A live progress banner shows transfer rate and time left while syncing, and a backup history records every past sync. Each telescope card shows when it last synced, and a failed sync gets its own panel with the full error text.

databaseBackup.title: Automatic database backups
databaseBackup.description: Nebulis snapshots its database automatically just before it applies a new version, so you can return to an earlier release without losing data. Make one yourself, or manage the rest, at Settings -> Storage -> Backups.

connectionMethodTabs.wifiBody: A SeeStar is usually <1>seestar.local</1> or the IP from its app. A Dwarf defaults to <3>192.168.88.1</3> only when it broadcasts its own access point; joined to your home Wi-Fi it takes whatever address your router assigns. A green result means you are ready to import.
connectionMethodTabs.wifiAlt: The hostname field filled in with seestar.local, and a green Connected result reading 'Connected. Found 209 object folders.'
connectionMethodTabs.usbBody: Plug the telescope's storage into this computer and tap the refresh icon to detect it, or type the path yourself if you already know it.
connectionMethodTabs.usbAlt: The USB storage path field with /Volumes/EMMC Images typed in

connectionMethodTabs.networkBody: For a NAS, a PC share, or another camera, pick <1>Other (custom SMB share)</1> as the telescope type, then enter the host and the share name.
